title: Introduction
content:
Introduction to the Hybrid Cloud System Hybrid Cloud is a model that combines on-premises enterprise network infrastructure with the AWS cloud computing environment. This model allows enterprises to leverage their existing network infrastructure while using cloud services to scale resources and deploy applications.
Site-to-Site VPN provides a secure connection between multi-branch enterprise networks and AWS through encrypted IPsec tunnels. This solution allows internal networks to exchange data with the cloud environment without exposing internal resources directly to the Internet.
Centralized Monitoring uses Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana to collect, monitor, and visualize server performance metrics. This enables administrators to monitor resource utilization, detect anomalies, and support troubleshooting.
Workshop Overview In this workshop, you will build a Hybrid Cloud model consisting of a multi-branch enterprise network simulated using EVE-NG and an AWS environment using Amazon VPC.
“On-premises Enterprise Network” simulates the network infrastructure at the headquarters and branch offices. Routers are configured to connect internal networks and establish Site-to-Site VPN connections with AWS.
“AWS Cloud Environment” uses Amazon VPC to deploy cloud network infrastructure, including subnets, an Internet Gateway, a Virtual Private Gateway, and route tables. Amazon EC2 instances are deployed to provide services and test connectivity between the two environments.
“Site-to-Site VPN Connectivity” uses IPsec tunnels to connect the enterprise network to AWS. Two VPN tunnels are configured to test connectivity and establish a backup mechanism in case of a connection failure.
“Centralized Monitoring System” is deployed on Amazon EC2, using Prometheus to collect metrics, Node Exporter to provide system resource information, and Grafana to display data through dashboards.
Through this workshop, you will practice designing a Hybrid Cloud architecture, deploying Site-to-Site VPN connectivity, configuring routing between networks, testing redundancy capabilities, and building a centralized monitoring system.

Overview of the Deployment Environment To deploy a Hybrid Cloud system that connects a multi-branch enterprise network using Site-to-Site VPN and integrates a centralized monitoring solution, we need to prepare both the on-premises network environment and the AWS cloud environment.
The on-premises environment is simulated using EVE-NG, which allows us to build an enterprise network consisting of multiple routers and internal networks at the headquarters and branch offices. AWS is used to deploy the cloud network infrastructure, establish VPN connectivity, and run servers that support centralized monitoring.
Required Components EVE-NG: Used to simulate the multi-branch enterprise network infrastructure, including routers, network devices, and internal LANs.
Amazon Web Services (AWS): Used to deploy the Hybrid Cloud infrastructure, including Amazon VPC, subnets, Internet Gateway, Virtual Private Gateway, route tables, and related resources.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN: Used to establish IPsec VPN tunnels connecting the on-premises network to AWS, ensuring secure data exchange between the two environments.
Amazon EC2: Used to deploy servers running web services and system monitoring components.
Prometheus and Node Exporter: Used to collect performance metrics and server resource utilization data.
Grafana: Used to visualize monitoring data through dashboards, enabling administrators to monitor system status.
Administration Computer: Used to configure network devices in EVE-NG, manage AWS resources, and access the monitoring interface through a web browser.

The main objectives of the event were:
To understand the role of APIs in connecting and exchanging data between system components. To explore important standards and principles for designing Backend APIs. To understand the importance of building APIs that are easy to use, maintain, and scale. To encourage continuous learning, knowledge sharing, and professional development within the technology community. 2. Speaker and Topic Nguyen Nhan – FCAJ Member: API Standards in Backend Development. 3. Key Topics 3.1. Overview of APIs in Backend Development An API (Application Programming Interface) allows applications or software components to communicate and exchange data with one another. In modern systems, APIs play an important role in connecting Frontend applications with Backend services, integrating services, and facilitating data exchange between different systems.
Key concepts include:
Understanding the concept of APIs and their role in software architecture. Recognizing how APIs enable communication between applications and services. Understanding the importance of designing APIs that are clear, consistent, and easy to use. Recognizing the role of APIs in integrating components within larger systems. 3.2. API Design Standards and Principles The session focused on important standards and principles for developing Backend APIs, with an emphasis on usability, maintainability, and scalability as systems grow.
Key aspects include:
Consistency: Using consistent endpoint naming conventions, data structures, and response formats. Usability: Designing clear endpoints that other applications and services can easily integrate with. Maintainability: Organizing APIs logically to simplify updates, bug fixes, and the development of new features. Scalability: Designing APIs with a structure that can accommodate future system growth. Compatibility: Minimizing breaking changes that could affect applications already using the APIs. These principles demonstrate that API development involves more than simply processing requests. It also requires attention to design quality and long-term maintainability.
3.3. The Role of APIs in Modern Systems As software systems become more complex, APIs become essential components that enable services to communicate and work together. Well-designed APIs can reduce dependencies between components, support integration, and facilitate future system development.
Important considerations when designing APIs include:
Clearly defining the purpose of each endpoint and the data it needs to exchange. Standardizing request handling, responses, and error messages. Prioritizing authentication, authorization, and data protection when exposing APIs. Considering API versioning when modifying or introducing new features. Providing clear API documentation to support development and integration. These principles can be applied when designing and developing software systems in real-world environments.

title: Project Proposal
content:
Design and Implementation of a Hybrid Cloud System Connecting Multi-Branch Enterprise Networks Using Site-to-Site VPN with Integrated Centralized Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The Hybrid Cloud System for Multi-Branch Enterprise Networks project aims to research and implement a connectivity model between an on-premises enterprise network infrastructure and the Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud platform.
The system adopts a Hybrid Cloud model, in which the enterprise network infrastructure is simulated using EVE-NG with Cisco networking devices, including routers, Cisco ASA firewalls, and LANs representing multiple branches. Connectivity between the on-premises network and AWS is established through AWS Site-to-Site VPN using IPsec, allowing internal networks to exchange data through encrypted tunnels.
In addition to network connectivity, the project integrates a centralized monitoring solution to monitor the operational status of servers, network devices, and system services. Prometheus is used to collect and store time-series monitoring data, Grafana provides visualization dashboards and alerting capabilities, while the ELK Stack supports centralized log collection, searching, and analysis.
The AWS infrastructure uses services such as Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Virtual Private Gateway, and Site-to-Site VPN. The architecture is designed to support future expansion to additional branches and to incorporate redundancy mechanisms that improve system availability.
2. Problem Statement Current Challenges In a multi-branch enterprise environment, connecting separate LANs and exchanging data with centralized servers introduces requirements for security, manageability, and network reliability.
When branches operate independently, accessing shared resources, managing servers, and troubleshooting network issues can become challenging. Distributed monitoring also increases the time required to detect and resolve incidents.
Furthermore, when an enterprise migrates part of its infrastructure to the cloud, a secure connectivity solution is required between the internal network and cloud resources. The solution must also provide appropriate routing, access control, and connection monitoring.
Proposed Solution The project develops a Hybrid Cloud model that connects a multi-branch enterprise network to AWS through Site-to-Site VPN.
The proposed solution consists of the following components:
Enterprise Network Infrastructure: EVE-NG is used to simulate routers, switches, Cisco ASA firewalls, and multiple LANs representing departments or branches. Hybrid Cloud Connectivity: Amazon VPC provides a private network environment on AWS, while AWS Site-to-Site VPN establishes IPsec connectivity between the enterprise network and a Virtual Private Gateway. Cloud Servers: Amazon EC2 instances host web applications, network services, or monitoring components as required. Routing and Redundancy: Routing is configured between internal networks and the VPC. Two VPN tunnels and appropriate failover mechanisms are used to improve connectivity resilience. Centralized Monitoring: Prometheus and Grafana monitor system metrics, while the ELK Stack centralizes and analyzes log data. Security: Firewall rules, Security Groups, Network ACLs where appropriate, routing policies, and access controls restrict unnecessary traffic. The model is implemented in a lab environment to test network connectivity, data exchange, cloud service access, monitoring, and troubleshooting procedures.
Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI) The project is expected to provide the following benefits:
Centrally connect branch networks to AWS resources through encrypted VPN tunnels. Support the use of on-premises infrastructure alongside cloud computing resources. Improve visibility into the operational status of servers and network devices. Reduce incident detection and troubleshooting time through dashboards, alerts, and centralized logs. Provide a practical environment for learning enterprise networking, security, cloud computing, and infrastructure monitoring. Establish an extensible foundation for additional branches, servers, and monitoring services. The project’s value will be assessed through technical performance, infrastructure reusability, incident response time, and operating costs. As this is a research and lab implementation project, financial benefits should be evaluated using actual results rather than an assumed fixed payback period.
3. Solution Architecture The system adopts a Hybrid Cloud architecture that combines an enterprise network simulated in EVE-NG with cloud resources hosted on AWS.
On the enterprise side, LANs are interconnected through routers and firewalls. Edge routers establish IPsec VPN connections to AWS. On the cloud side, Amazon VPC provides a private network environment containing subnets and EC2 instances configured according to their intended roles.
The main connectivity flow is as follows:
Users in enterprise LANs access internal resources or servers hosted on AWS. Traffic destined for cloud networks is routed through the edge routers and firewalls according to the configured network policies. The routers establish IPsec tunnels to AWS Site-to-Site VPN. AWS receives traffic through the Virtual Private Gateway and routes it to the destination subnets. AWS-hosted servers provide services according to their Security Group rules and network configurations. The monitoring system collects data from supported servers and components. Metrics are displayed in Grafana dashboards, while ELK Stack supports log analysis. AWS Services and Technologies EVE-NG: Simulates the enterprise network infrastructure, including routers, switches, firewalls, and multiple LANs. Cisco IOS and Cisco ASA: Configure routing, firewall policies, NAT, and traffic control. Amazon VPC: Provides a private network environment on AWS, including subnets and route tables. AWS Site-to-Site VPN: Establishes IPsec connectivity between the enterprise network and AWS. Virtual Private Gateway: Provides the AWS-side VPN endpoint attached to the VPC. Amazon EC2: Hosts application servers and monitoring components. Amazon VPC Route Tables: Control traffic routing between subnets and enterprise networks connected through the VPN. Prometheus: Collects performance metrics and status information from configured servers and services. Grafana: Visualizes metrics through dashboards and supports alert configuration. ELK Stack: Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana provide log storage, processing, searching, and analysis. AWS CloudWatch: Monitors metrics and logs from supported AWS services. Component Design Enterprise Network Infrastructure
The network model contains LANs representing different departments or branches. Routers and firewalls handle routing, traffic control, and forwarding between networks.
VPN Connectivity Layer
AWS Site-to-Site VPN provides IPsec tunnels for secure data transmission between the enterprise network and the VPC. The project examines a two-tunnel configuration and routing failover mechanisms to maintain connectivity when one tunnel becomes unavailable.
AWS Infrastructure
Amazon VPC provides a private IP address space. Subnets are organized according to their functions and access policies. Amazon EC2 instances host web services or monitoring components, depending on the implementation phase.
Monitoring System
Prometheus collects metrics from compatible exporters or monitoring endpoints. Grafana displays CPU usage, memory utilization, disk capacity, service status, and available network metrics. The ELK Stack centralizes and analyzes logs from servers and devices capable of exporting compatible log data.
Security Layer
Firewalls, Security Groups, and routing policies follow the principle of allowing only necessary traffic. Administrative protocols and monitoring interfaces are restricted to appropriate sources to avoid unnecessary exposure to the public Internet.
4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases The project is divided into four main phases.
Phase 1: Research and Architecture Design
Study Hybrid Cloud architecture and multi-branch enterprise connectivity requirements. Research the operating principles of IPsec VPN and AWS Site-to-Site VPN. Design the EVE-NG network topology, identifying LANs, edge routers, firewalls, and AWS network components. Develop the IP addressing plan, routing tables, and redundancy strategy. Phase 2: Infrastructure Setup and VPN Configuration
Deploy network devices and configure IP addresses in EVE-NG. Configure internal routing, default routes, and necessary NAT policies. Create the VPC, subnets, Virtual Private Gateway, and VPN connection on AWS. Configure routers to establish IPsec tunnels. Verify tunnel status, test connectivity to VPN tunnel endpoints, and validate communication between permitted networks. Phase 3: Cloud Server and Monitoring Deployment
Deploy EC2 instances for web applications or other required services. Configure Prometheus to collect metrics from monitoring endpoints. Deploy Grafana and build dashboards for system resource monitoring. Deploy the ELK Stack when sufficient resources are available, and configure log collection and analysis. Verify administrative connectivity and monitoring traffic flows through the VPN according to the architecture. Phase 4: Testing, Optimization, and Documentation
Test connectivity between LANs and AWS resources. Verify service access according to firewall and Security Group policies. Simulate VPN tunnel failures to evaluate routing failover. Test metric collection, dashboard visualization, and log analysis. Optimize network configuration, access permissions, and cloud resources. Complete the architecture diagrams, IP addressing tables, device configurations, and test reports. Technical Requirements Network Infrastructure
Use EVE-NG and a virtualization environment to build the network topology. Configure routers, Cisco ASA firewalls, LANs, and WAN connectivity. Maintain a clear IP addressing plan and avoid overlapping networks. Configure bidirectional routing between the enterprise network and the VPC. Test routing failover when two VPN tunnels are configured. AWS Infrastructure
Use Amazon VPC and subnets appropriate to the architecture. Create a Virtual Private Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. Configure route tables to direct traffic to enterprise networks through the VPN. Deploy EC2 instances according to actual requirements and budget constraints. Configure Security Groups to allow only the necessary service ports. Monitoring System
Install Prometheus to collect metrics from servers or compatible exporters. Use Grafana to build dashboards and configure alerts. Deploy the ELK Stack when resources permit centralized log collection and analysis. Monitor CPU, memory, disk capacity, and network utilization. Restrict access to administrative interfaces and monitoring dashboards. 5. Implementation Timeline and Milestones The project follows a series of milestones during the internship period from August 10 to December 1.
Phase 1 – Research and Design: Study Hybrid Cloud technologies, design the network topology, plan IP addressing, and develop the AWS connectivity architecture. Phase 2 – Network Infrastructure Setup: Build the EVE-NG topology, configure routers and firewalls, and verify internal connectivity. Phase 3 – AWS VPN Deployment: Create the VPC, subnets, Virtual Private Gateway, and VPN connection; configure tunnels and routing between both environments. Phase 4 – Cloud Server Deployment: Launch EC2 instances and verify service access from permitted networks. Phase 5 – Monitoring Integration: Deploy Prometheus, Grafana, and the ELK Stack according to available resources; verify metric and log collection. Phase 6 – Testing and Finalization: Test connectivity, redundancy, security, and performance, then complete the project documentation. After the internship, the model can be extended to explore configuration automation, advanced alerting, centralized configuration management, and additional cloud security mechanisms.
6. Estimated Budget The project’s cost depends on VPN usage duration, the number of EC2 instances, storage capacity, data transfer volume, and the resources allocated to monitoring tools.
The AWS Pricing Calculator can be used to estimate costs based on the actual deployment configuration.
Cost Components Amazon EC2: Costs for application servers or monitoring instances, depending on instance type and running time. Amazon EBS: Costs for storage volumes attached to EC2 instances. AWS Site-to-Site VPN: VPN connection charges and applicable data transfer costs. Amazon VPC: Core components such as VPCs, subnets, and route tables generally do not incur separate charges; related resources may incur additional fees. Amazon CloudWatch: Charges may apply when usage exceeds the applicable free usage allowances for metrics, logs, or alarms. Prometheus and Grafana: The software can run on EC2, but the underlying compute and storage resources still incur costs. ELK Stack: CPU, memory, disk capacity, and log storage costs must be considered when deploying on EC2. EVE-NG and Virtualization Environment: Existing personal computer resources are used; electricity and hardware costs may be considered where applicable. Cost Optimization Strategies Start EC2 instances only when performing configuration, testing, or demonstrations. Select instance types that match the required workload and available resources. Monitor AWS Billing and configure budget alerts. Remove unused resources after checking for dependencies and resources that may continue to incur charges. Deploy monitoring tools incrementally to avoid running multiple resource-intensive services simultaneously. Do not assume that costs are zero simply because an instance is covered by a free usage allowance or promotional credits. The final budget should be validated using the AWS Pricing Calculator and actual billing data. VPN charges and monitoring infrastructure costs should be evaluated separately rather than estimating the project solely from EC2 instance costs.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix VPN Connectivity Failure: High impact; may result from incorrect IPsec configuration, routing errors, or network interruptions. Routing Misconfiguration: High impact; may prevent communication between branch networks and cloud resources. Unauthorized Access: High impact if firewalls, Security Groups, or administrative interfaces are configured insecurely. Insufficient Monitoring Resources: Medium to high impact when EC2 instances lack adequate CPU, memory, or storage. AWS Budget Overrun: Medium to high impact if billable resources remain active beyond the testing period. Log Data Loss: Medium impact if appropriate retention and backup policies are not implemented. Risk Mitigation Strategies VPN: Verify tunnel status, IKE/IPsec parameters, peer addresses, access control lists, and routing tables. Configure two tunnels and test failover behavior. Routing: Maintain an IP addressing plan, identify source and destination networks, verify bidirectional paths, and use traceroute or equivalent diagnostic tools. Security: Restrict SSH, monitoring ports, and administrative interfaces to approved sources. Avoid unnecessarily permissive rules. Resources: Monitor CPU, memory, disk usage, and adjust configurations according to workload requirements. Costs: Configure budget alerts, review active resources, and stop or remove resources that are no longer needed. Logs: Define retention policies, manage storage capacity, and back up important data. Contingency Plan If one VPN tunnel fails, the system will be tested to determine whether traffic can move to the remaining tunnel according to the configured routing mechanism. If the VPN cannot be restored, troubleshooting will proceed through each layer, including WAN connectivity, IPsec status, internal routing, and AWS route tables.
For the monitoring system, Prometheus, Grafana, and ELK configurations should be preserved to support recovery after failures. Network and AWS configurations can be documented or stored as infrastructure code to facilitate redeployment when necessary.
8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements Build a Hybrid Cloud model connecting an enterprise network to AWS through Site-to-Site VPN. Establish connectivity between internal networks and VPC resources according to routing policies. Test two VPN tunnels and routing failover when a failure occurs. Deploy EC2 instances for applications or required services. Build monitoring dashboards for server resources using Prometheus and Grafana. Integrate the ELK Stack for log collection, searching, and analysis when sufficient resources are available. Complete network diagrams, IP addressing tables, VPN configurations, security rules, and testing procedures. Long-Term Value The project establishes a practical foundation for studying enterprise network administration, cloud computing, secure connectivity, and centralized monitoring. The architecture can be extended to connect additional branches, deploy more servers, improve redundancy, and introduce infrastructure management automation.
Through this project, the implementer can apply computer networking knowledge to cloud environments and improve practical skills in network device configuration, IPsec VPN deployment, AWS resource management, and infrastructure monitoring.
The final results will be evaluated based on actual connectivity, VPN tunnel status, routing correctness, service accessibility under security policies, and monitoring data collection.

title: Design and Deployment of AWS Network Infrastructure
content:
Overview of AWS Network Infrastructure In the Hybrid Cloud model, Amazon Web Services (AWS) provides a cloud computing environment that connects to the enterprise network simulated in EVE-NG. The AWS network infrastructure is designed to provide connectivity between cloud-based servers and internal networks at the headquarters and branch offices.
The main network components include Amazon VPC, subnets, Internet Gateway, and route tables. In addition, a Virtual Private Gateway is used to establish a Site-to-Site VPN connection between AWS and the on-premises network.
Deployment Objectives Create and configure an Amazon VPC with an appropriate IP address range. Build a public subnet to deploy Amazon EC2 instances. Connect the VPC to the Internet through an Internet Gateway. Configure route tables to control network traffic between AWS, the Internet, and the enterprise network. Prepare a Virtual Private Gateway for the Site-to-Site VPN connection. IP Addressing Design The AWS network infrastructure uses the private IP address range 10.100.0.0/16. This range is selected to avoid overlapping with the internal networks in the on-premises environment.
Component Resource Name IP Range / Configuration Amazon VPC HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC 10.100.0.0/16 Public Subnet AWS-PUBLIC-SUBNET 10.100.1.0/24 Internet Gateway HYBRID-CLOUD-IGW Connects the VPC to the Internet Virtual Private Gateway VGW Supports the Site-to-Site VPN connection Route Table AWS-PUBLIC-RT Controls routing for the public subnet Deploying Amazon VPC Amazon VPC is a logically isolated virtual network in AWS that allows administrators to control IP address ranges, subnets, routing, and network connectivity.
Follow these steps:
Access the AWS Management Console. Open the Amazon VPC service. Select Your VPCs, then click Create VPC. Create a VPC and enter HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC as the name. Enter 10.100.0.0/16 as the IPv4 CIDR block. Keep the other settings according to the lab requirements. Click Create VPC to complete the process. [Insert image here: AWS console interface for creating an Amazon VPC]
After the VPC is created successfully, verify its name and IPv4 address range in the Your VPCs list.
Creating a Public Subnet A public subnet is used to deploy servers that require Internet connectivity, such as a web server and a monitoring server.
Follow these steps:
In the Amazon VPC console, select Subnets. Click Create subnet. Select the VPC HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC. Set the subnet name to AWS-PUBLIC-SUBNET. Select an appropriate Availability Zone, such as us-east-1b. Enter 10.100.1.0/24 as the IPv4 subnet CIDR block. Click Create subnet. Select the newly created subnet, open Actions, and enable Enable auto-assign public IPv4 address if new EC2 instances should automatically receive public IPv4 addresses. [Insert image here: AWS console configuration for creating the public subnet]
Note: Enabling automatic public IPv4 address assignment does not replace the need to configure an Internet Gateway and route table.
Creating and Attaching an Internet Gateway An Internet Gateway allows resources in a VPC to communicate with the Internet when the appropriate routing and security configurations are in place.
Follow these steps:
In the Amazon VPC console, select Internet gateways. Click Create internet gateway. Set the name to HYBRID-CLOUD-IGW. Click Create internet gateway. Select the newly created Internet Gateway. Open Actions and select Attach to a VPC. Select HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC and confirm the attachment. [Insert image here: Internet Gateway successfully created and attached to the VPC]
After completing these steps, verify that the Internet Gateway is attached to the VPC.
Configuring the Route Table A route table determines where network traffic is directed. In this model, the public route table is used to route Internet traffic and traffic destined for enterprise networks through the VPN.
Follow these steps:
In the Amazon VPC console, select Route tables. Create or select the route table named AWS-PUBLIC-RT. Ensure that the route table belongs to HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC. Open the Routes tab and select Edit routes. Add the route 0.0.0.0/0 with HYBRID-CLOUD-IGW as the target. Add routes to the enterprise networks through the Virtual Private Gateway after the VPN has been created and configured, using the actual network ranges in the lab. Save the changes and open the Subnet associations tab. Associate AWS-PUBLIC-SUBNET with AWS-PUBLIC-RT. [Insert image here: AWS-PUBLIC-RT route table with the default route pointing to the Internet Gateway]
Routes to on-premises networks will work only after the VPN and the corresponding routing configuration are ready. Do not add network ranges that are not used in the actual environment.
Verifying the Deployment After completing the configuration, verify the following:
The Amazon VPC uses the CIDR block 10.100.0.0/16. The public subnet uses the CIDR block 10.100.1.0/24. The Internet Gateway is attached to the VPC. The route table contains the default route 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the Internet Gateway. The public subnet is associated with the appropriate route table. Routes to enterprise networks are added when the Site-to-Site VPN has been configured. [Insert image here: Overview of the configured VPC, subnet, Internet Gateway, and route table]
Expected Results After completing this section, the basic AWS network infrastructure will be ready for deploying EC2 instances and integrating with the enterprise network. Amazon VPC, the public subnet, the Internet Gateway, and the route table provide the foundation for deploying cloud services.
In the next section, we will configure an Amazon EC2 instance and its Security Groups to deploy the services required for the Hybrid Cloud system.

title: Deployment of Amazon EC2 and Security Group Configuration
content:
Overview of Amazon EC2 Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is an AWS service that provides virtual servers in the cloud. In the Hybrid Cloud model, EC2 is used to deploy essential services, including web servers and system monitoring components.
In this project, an EC2 instance running Ubuntu Server 24.04 is deployed in the public subnet of the HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC. This instance is used to run Nginx, Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana for testing and monitoring purposes.
Deployment Objectives Create an EC2 instance in the AWS public subnet. Use Ubuntu Server 24.04 as the operating system. Configure Security Groups to control inbound traffic to the instance. Connect to the EC2 instance through SSH. Install and verify the Nginx service. Prepare the environment for deploying centralized monitoring components. EC2 Instance Specifications Component Configuration Instance Name HYBRID-CLOUD-WEBSERVER-SG Operating System Ubuntu Server 24.04 Instance Type t3.micro VPC HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC Subnet AWS-PUBLIC-SUBNET Private IPv4 Address 10.100.1.118 Root Volume 8 GiB gp3 Web Server Nginx Monitoring Components Prometheus, Node Exporter, Grafana [Insert image here: EC2 instance details in the AWS Management Console]
Note: The public IPv4 address of an EC2 instance may change after the instance is stopped and started if an Elastic IP is not assigned. Before accessing the services, check the current public IP address in the AWS Console.
Deploying an EC2 Instance Follow these steps:
Access the AWS Management Console. Open the Amazon EC2 service. Select Instances, then click Launch instances. Enter HYBRID-CLOUD-WEBSERVER-SG as the instance name. Select Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS as the operating system. Select the t3.micro instance type if it is suitable for the available limits and budget. Create or select a key pair for SSH access. Under Network settings, select the VPC HYBRID-CLOUD-VPC. Select the subnet AWS-PUBLIC-SUBNET. Configure an appropriate Security Group for the services to be deployed. Configure the storage capacity according to the requirements, for example, an 8 GiB gp3 volume. Review the configuration and click Launch instance. [Insert image here: Launch instance configuration in the AWS Console]
After launching the instance, verify that its state is Running and that the instance status checks have passed before connecting.
Configuring Security Groups A Security Group acts as a virtual firewall at the AWS resource level, controlling inbound and outbound traffic for an EC2 instance.
For this project, inbound rules should follow the principle of allowing only the connections that are actually required.
Type Protocol Port Range Source Purpose SSH TCP 22 My IP /32 Remote server administration HTTP TCP 80 0.0.0.0/0 Access to the Nginx website Custom TCP TCP 3000 My IP /32 or management network Access to Grafana when required Custom TCP TCP 9090 My IP /32 or monitoring network Access to Prometheus when required Custom TCP TCP 9100 Prometheus server or monitoring network only Collect metrics from Node Exporter [Insert image here: Security Group inbound rules in the AWS Console]
Security considerations:
Do not expose SSH port 22 to the entire Internet unless absolutely necessary. Allow access to monitoring ports only from authorized IP addresses or management networks. Do not expose port 9100 publicly because Node Exporter provides system monitoring information. Inbound rules must match the actual deployment architecture. If services are accessible only through the VPN, restrict their sources to the corresponding internal network ranges. Security Groups are stateful, so response traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted. Connecting to the EC2 Instance Using SSH Once the EC2 instance is running properly, use SSH to administer the Ubuntu operating system.
On a Windows computer, open PowerShell and navigate to the directory containing the private key. Run the following command, replacing the key path and IP address with the actual values:
ssh -i "hybrid-cloud-webserver-key.pem" ubuntu@<PUBLIC_IP>

title: Site-to-Site VPN Configuration for Multi-Branch Enterprise Networks
content:
Overview In this section, we will configure an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to securely connect the on-premises enterprise network simulated in EVE-NG with the AWS cloud environment.
The solution uses an AWS Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) attached to the Hybrid Cloud VPC and a Customer Gateway representing the on-premises VPN device. The IPsec VPN tunnels provide encrypted communication between the enterprise network and AWS.
The enterprise network includes a headquarters and multiple branch offices. The VPN connection allows authorized internal networks to communicate with resources deployed in the AWS VPC.
1. Prepare the VPN Environment Before creating the VPN connection, verify that the following resources and information are available:
An existing AWS VPC. A Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) attached to the VPC. The public IP address reachable by AWS for the on-premises VPN device. The on-premises network CIDR ranges. The AWS VPC CIDR range. An operational edge router or VPN device in EVE-NG. For this project, the AWS VPC uses the CIDR range 10.100.0.0/16. The on-premises network ranges must match the actual enterprise network configuration.
Image 1: AWS VPC and Virtual Private Gateway
2. Create a Customer Gateway A Customer Gateway represents the on-premises VPN device in AWS.
Open the AWS Management Console. Navigate to VPC. In the navigation pane, select Customer Gateways. Choose Create customer gateway. Enter a descriptive name, such as HYBRID-CLOUD-CGW. Select Routing according to the routing design. For this lab, use static routing if the VPN configuration uses static routes. Select the appropriate BGP ASN only if dynamic BGP routing is being used. Enter the public IP address reachable by AWS for the on-premises VPN device. Choose Create customer gateway. Note: The Customer Gateway IP must be reachable from AWS over the Internet. Do not enter a private VMnet8 address such as 192.168.80.x as the public VPN endpoint.
Image 2: Create Customer Gateway
3. Create a Site-to-Site VPN Connection After creating the Customer Gateway, create the VPN connection.
In the VPC console, select Site-to-Site VPN Connections. Choose Create VPN connection. Enter the VPN connection name, such as HYBRID-CLOUD-S2S-VPN. Select the existing Virtual Private Gateway. Select the Customer Gateway created in the previous step. Choose the routing option that matches the on-premises configuration. If using static routing, add the on-premises network CIDR ranges. Review the configuration and choose Create VPN connection. AWS creates two IPsec VPN tunnels for the connection. These tunnels provide alternative paths between the on-premises network and AWS.
Image 3: Create Site-to-Site VPN Connection
4. Download the VPN Configuration AWS provides a configuration file containing the tunnel parameters and example device configuration.
Select the newly created VPN connection. Choose Download configuration. Select the appropriate vendor and platform for the on-premises VPN device, if available. Download the configuration file. Review the outside tunnel IP addresses, inside tunnel IP addresses, pre-shared keys, encryption algorithms, and other IPsec parameters. The downloaded configuration is used as a reference when configuring the VPN device in EVE-NG.
Important: Keep the pre-shared keys confidential. Do not publish them in screenshots, source files, or public repositories.
Image 4: Download VPN Configuration
5. Configure the VPN Tunnel on the On-Premises Router Use the downloaded AWS configuration as a reference to configure the on-premises router in EVE-NG.
The configuration must match the parameters provided by AWS, including:
Outside tunnel IP address. Inside tunnel IP address. Pre-shared key. IKE version and authentication settings. Encryption and integrity algorithms. Diffie-Hellman group. IPsec lifetime and related parameters. Configure both AWS-provided tunnels on the appropriate on-premises VPN device.
Note: The exact commands depend on the router model and operating system. Use the configuration generated by AWS rather than copying example commands with different tunnel parameters.
Image 5: Configure IPsec VPN on the EVE-NG Router
6. Configure Routing Between the On-Premises Network and AWS To allow communication between the two environments, configure routing on both sides.
On the AWS side:
Open the VPC console. Select Route Tables. Open the route table associated with the subnets that need to communicate with the on-premises network. Choose Edit routes. Add the on-premises network CIDR ranges. Set the target to the Virtual Private Gateway. Save the changes. On the on-premises side:
Configure routes to the AWS VPC CIDR range 10.100.0.0/16. Set the next hop or tunnel interface according to the VPN design. Verify that the internal routers can forward traffic toward the VPN device. Ensure that the on-premises network CIDRs do not overlap with the AWS VPC CIDR.
Image 6: Configure AWS Route Table
Image 7: Configure Routes on the On-Premises Router
7. Verify the VPN Tunnel Status After completing the configuration, verify the status of the VPN tunnels.
Open Site-to-Site VPN Connections in the VPC console. Select the VPN connection. Open the Tunnel details tab. Check the status of both tunnels. Confirm that the expected tunnel status is UP. On the EVE-NG router, use the appropriate commands to check the IKE and IPsec security associations and tunnel interfaces.
Example verification commands for Cisco IOS:
show crypto isakmp sa show crypto ipsec sa show interface tunnel show ip route The exact commands may vary depending on the router platform and VPN configuration.
Image 8: AWS VPN Tunnel Status
Image 9: Verify IPsec Status on the Router
Conclusion In this section, we created an AWS Customer Gateway and Site-to-Site VPN connection, configured the IPsec tunnels on the on-premises VPN device, and established routing between the enterprise network and the AWS VPC.
The VPN connection provides an encrypted communication path between the on-premises infrastructure and the cloud environment. In the next section, we will configure routing and VPN failover mechanisms to improve connectivity availability.

title: Workshop
content:
Design and Implementation of a Hybrid Cloud System Connecting Multi-Branch Enterprise Networks via Site-to-Site VPN Integrated with a Centralized Monitoring Solution Overview In this workshop, we will learn how to design and implement a Hybrid Cloud system connecting multi-branch enterprise networks via Site-to-Site VPN integrated with a centralized monitoring solution.
The system uses EVE-NG to simulate the on-premises enterprise network infrastructure and Amazon Web Services (AWS) to build the cloud environment. The internal networks at the headquarters and branch offices connect to AWS through IPsec-based Site-to-Site VPN tunnels, enabling secure communication between the two environments.
The system also implements redundant routing to improve network availability. For centralized monitoring, Prometheus and Node Exporter collect server performance metrics, while Grafana visualizes the collected data through dashboards.
Through this workshop, we will build a Hybrid Cloud network infrastructure, establish secure VPN connections, configure routing between networks, test connectivity and failover, and deploy a centralized monitoring solution.
Objectives Hybrid Cloud Architecture: Design connectivity between multi-branch enterprise networks and AWS. AWS Network Infrastructure: Configure Amazon VPC, subnets, Internet Gateway, Virtual Private Gateway, and route tables. Amazon EC2 and Security: Deploy an EC2 instance and configure Security Groups. Site-to-Site VPN: Establish IPsec VPN tunnels between the on-premises network and AWS. Routing and Failover: Configure routes, test connectivity, and verify VPN redundancy. Centralized Monitoring: Deploy Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana. System Testing: Validate connectivity, VPN operation, failover, and monitoring. Contents Hybrid Cloud Architecture Overview Deployment Environment Preparation AWS Network Infrastructure Design and Deployment Amazon EC2 Deployment and Security Group Configuration Site-to-Site VPN Configuration for Multi-Branch Enterprise Networks Routing Configuration and VPN Failover Mechanisms Centralized Monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana Hybrid Cloud System Testing and AWS Resource Cleanup

title: Routing Configuration and VPN Failover Mechanisms
content:
Overview In this section, we will configure routing and VPN failover mechanisms to improve the availability of the Hybrid Cloud network.
The network uses two on-premises routers connected to AWS through separate Site-to-Site VPN connections. Router15 acts as the primary router, while Router16 provides a backup connection.
The primary VPN path is preferred during normal operation. If the primary path becomes unavailable, traffic is expected to use the backup VPN path. This design helps maintain communication between the enterprise network and AWS when a VPN tunnel or primary router fails.
1. Review the Network Topology Before configuring routing, review the Hybrid Cloud topology and identify the primary and backup paths.
The design includes:
Router15: Primary on-premises VPN router. Router16: Backup on-premises VPN router. AWS Virtual Private Gateway: Terminates the AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections. Primary VPN connection: Connects Router15 to AWS. Backup VPN connection: Connects Router16 to AWS. Enterprise internal networks: Headquarters and branch office networks. AWS VPC: Cloud network using CIDR 10.100.0.0/16. Each Customer Gateway must represent the correct public endpoint of its corresponding on-premises VPN device.
Image 1: Hybrid Cloud Primary and Backup VPN Topology
2. Configure the Primary VPN Route Configure Router15 as the preferred path to the AWS VPC.
The routing design should ensure that traffic destined for 10.100.0.0/16 uses the primary VPN tunnel under normal conditions.
For a Cisco router using static routing, a route can be configured with a tracking object:
ip route 10.100.0.0 255.255.0.0 Tunnel1 track 100 The tracking object must monitor a destination that is reachable through the primary VPN path. Configure the tracking mechanism according to the actual tunnel interface and network topology.
Image 2: Primary VPN Routing Configuration
3. Configure the Backup VPN Route Router16 provides an alternative path to AWS when the primary connection fails.
Configure a backup route with a higher administrative distance so that it is not selected while the primary route is available.
Example:
ip route 10.100.0.0 255.255.0.0 <BACKUP_NEXT_HOP> 10 Replace <BACKUP_NEXT_HOP> with the correct next-hop address or interface for the backup VPN path.
If both routers participate in a shared internal routing domain, ensure that route advertisement and route preference are configured consistently. The backup path must be reachable when the primary route is withdrawn.
Image 3: Backup VPN Routing Configuration
4. Configure Route Tracking and Failover Route tracking allows the router to detect whether the primary path is still usable.
For Cisco IOS, IP SLA and object tracking can be used to monitor reachability through the primary path.
Example configuration:
ip sla 1 icmp-echo <REACHABLE_DESTINATION> source-interface <SOURCE_INTERFACE> frequency 5 exit ip sla schedule 1 life forever start-time now track 100 ip sla 1 reachability The destination and source interface must be selected according to the actual network design. The monitoring destination should be reachable through the primary path and should not be reachable through an unrelated route that could hide a primary VPN failure.
Associate the tracking object with the primary static route. When the tracked path becomes unavailable, the primary route is removed from the routing table, allowing the backup route to be selected.
Image 4: IP SLA and Object Tracking Configuration
5. Verify the Routing Table After configuring the primary and backup routes, verify which path is currently selected.
On the Cisco router, use:
show ip route 10.100.0.0 show track 100 show ip sla statistics During normal operation, confirm that the route to 10.100.0.0/16 uses the primary VPN path.
Also verify that the backup route is available and can be installed when the primary route is withdrawn.
Image 5: Verify the Primary Route
6. Test VPN Failover Perform a controlled failover test to verify that the backup path works correctly.
Confirm that the primary VPN connection is operational. Verify connectivity from an on-premises host to an AWS resource. Record the current routing table. Temporarily disable the primary VPN path in the lab. Wait for the tracking mechanism to detect the failure. Verify that the primary route is withdrawn. Confirm that traffic uses the backup VPN path. Test connectivity to the AWS resource again. Restore the primary VPN path and verify that normal route preference is recovered. Use the following commands to check routing and connectivity:
show ip route 10.100.0.0 show track 100 show crypto ipsec sa ping <AWS_PRIVATE_IP> The test should demonstrate that traffic can use the backup path when the primary path is unavailable.
Image 6: Primary VPN Failure Test
Image 7: Backup VPN Path After Failover
7. Restore the Primary Path and Verify Recovery After completing the failover test:
Re-enable the primary VPN path. Wait for the VPN tunnel and tracking object to recover. Check the routing table again. Confirm that the primary route is preferred. Test connectivity between the on-premises network and AWS. This step verifies that the routing design can recover after a temporary failure.
Image 8: Primary VPN Path Recovery
Conclusion In this section, we configured primary and backup VPN routing, implemented route tracking, and tested failover and recovery between the on-premises enterprise network and AWS.
Router15 provides the preferred VPN path, while Router16 acts as the backup path. The failover mechanism improves network availability by allowing traffic to use the alternative connection when the primary path becomes unavailable.
In the next section, we will deploy a centralized monitoring solution using Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana.

title: Centralized Monitoring Deployment with Prometheus and Grafana
content:
Overview In this section, we will deploy a centralized monitoring solution to monitor the performance and resource utilization of the cloud server in the Hybrid Cloud environment.
The monitoring system is deployed on an Ubuntu 24.04 EC2 instance and consists of three main components:
Prometheus: Collects and stores time-series monitoring metrics. Node Exporter: Exposes Linux server metrics, including CPU, memory, disk, and network information. Grafana: Visualizes monitoring data through dashboards and charts. The components work together to help administrators observe server performance, identify resource usage trends, and detect potential infrastructure issues.
1. Prepare the Monitoring Environment Before installing the monitoring components, connect to the EC2 instance using SSH.
Use the following command from your local terminal:
ssh -i "hybrid-cloud-webserver-key.pem" ubuntu@<EC2_PUBLIC_IP> Replace <EC2_PUBLIC_IP> with the current public IPv4 address of the EC2 instance.
Update the Ubuntu package index:
sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade -y Check the operating system version:
lsb_release -a Confirm that the instance is running Ubuntu 24.04.
Image 1: Connect to the EC2 Instance
2. Install Node Exporter Node Exporter collects hardware and operating system metrics from Linux servers and exposes them for Prometheus to scrape.
Create a dedicated system user:
sudo useradd --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin node_exporter Download and extract Node Exporter:
cd /tmp wget https://github.com/prometheus/node_exporter/releases/download/v1.7.0/node_exporter-1.7.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz tar xvf node_exporter-1.7.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz Install the executable:
sudo cp node_exporter-1.7.0.linux-amd64/node_exporter /usr/local/bin/ sudo chown node_exporter:node_exporter /usr/local/bin/node_exporter Create a systemd service:
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/node_exporter.service Add the following configuration:
[Unit] Description=Node Exporter After=network.target [Service] User=node_exporter Group=node_exporter Type=simple ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/node_exporter [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Save the file and start the service:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now node_exporter Check the service status:
sudo systemctl status node_exporter Node Exporter uses TCP port 9100 by default.
Image 2: Node Exporter Installation and Service Status
3. Install Prometheus Prometheus is responsible for collecting and storing monitoring metrics from Node Exporter.
Create a dedicated system user and required directories:
sudo useradd --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin prometheus sudo mkdir -p /etc/prometheus sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/prometheus Download and extract Prometheus:
cd /tmp wget https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/releases/download/v2.54.1/prometheus-2.54.1.linux-amd64.tar.gz tar xvf prometheus-2.54.1.linux-amd64.tar.gz Copy the required files:
sudo cp prometheus-2.54.1.linux-amd64/prometheus /usr/local/bin/ sudo cp prometheus-2.54.1.linux-amd64/promtool /usr/local/bin/ sudo cp -r prometheus-2.54.1.linux-amd64/consoles /etc/prometheus/ sudo cp -r prometheus-2.54.1.linux-amd64/console_libraries /etc/prometheus/ Set the appropriate ownership:
sudo chown prometheus:prometheus /usr/local/bin/prometheus sudo chown prometheus:prometheus /usr/local/bin/promtool sudo chown -R prometheus:prometheus /etc/prometheus sudo chown -R prometheus:prometheus /var/lib/prometheus Image 3: Prometheus Installation
4. Configure Prometheus Create the Prometheus configuration file:
sudo nano /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml Add the following configuration:
global: scrape_interval: 15s scrape_configs: - job_name: "prometheus" static_configs: - targets: ["localhost:9090"] - job_name: "node_exporter" static_configs: - targets: ["localhost:9100"] This configuration defines two monitoring targets:
localhost:9090: Prometheus monitors its own metrics. localhost:9100: Prometheus collects Linux server metrics from Node Exporter. Set the configuration file ownership:
sudo chown prometheus:prometheus /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml Create a systemd service:
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/prometheus.service Add:
[Unit] Description=Prometheus Monitoring Wants=network-online.target After=network-online.target [Service] User=prometheus Group=prometheus Type=simple ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/prometheus \ --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml \ --storage.tsdb.path=/var/lib/prometheus/ \ --web.listen-address=0.0.0.0:9090 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Start and enable Prometheus:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now prometheus Check the service:
sudo systemctl status prometheus Image 4: Prometheus Configuration
Image 5: Prometheus Service Status
5. Verify Prometheus Targets Open the following address in a web browser:
http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>:9090/targets Replace <EC2_PUBLIC_IP> with the public IPv4 address of the EC2 instance.
The Targets page should display the configured monitoring endpoints.
Verify that both targets have the status UP:
prometheus node_exporter If a target is DOWN, check the corresponding service and Prometheus configuration.
Image 6: Prometheus Targets Status
6. Install Grafana Grafana provides dashboards for visualizing the metrics collected by Prometheus.
Install the required packages:
sudo apt-get install -y apt-transport-https software-properties-common wget Create the keyrings directory:
sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings Add the Grafana package signing key:
wget -q -O - https://apt.grafana.com/gpg.key | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.gpg > /dev/null Add the Grafana repository:
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.gpg] https://apt.grafana.com stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/grafana.list Update the package index and install Grafana:
sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y grafana Enable and start Grafana:
sudo systemctl enable --now grafana-server Check the service status:
sudo systemctl status grafana-server Grafana uses TCP port 3000 by default.
Image 7: Grafana Installation and Service Status
7. Access Grafana and Add Prometheus as a Data Source Open Grafana in a web browser:
http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>:3000 Log in using the configured administrator credentials. On a fresh installation, the default credentials are:
Username: admin Password: admin Grafana will normally require changing the default password after the first login.
To add Prometheus as a data source:
Open Connections. Select Data sources. Choose Add data source. Select Prometheus. Enter the Prometheus server URL: http://localhost:9090 Choose Save & test. Confirm that Grafana can successfully connect to Prometheus.
Image 8: Add Prometheus Data Source in Grafana
8. Create a Monitoring Dashboard After adding Prometheus as a data source, create a dashboard to visualize server performance.
Open Dashboards. Select New. Choose New dashboard. Add a visualization. Select Prometheus as the data source. Enter a PromQL query. Save the dashboard. Example PromQL queries:
CPU Usage:
100 * (1 - avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]))) Memory Usage:
100 * (1 - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes) Disk Usage:
100 * (1 - node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/",fstype!="tmpfs"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/",fstype!="tmpfs"}) Network Receive Traffic:
rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{device!="lo"}[5m]) The dashboard can display CPU utilization, memory consumption, disk usage, and network traffic.
Image 9: Grafana Monitoring Dashboard
9. Test the Monitoring System To verify that the monitoring system collects real-time metrics, generate a temporary CPU workload on the EC2 instance.
Install stress-ng if it is not already installed:
sudo apt update sudo apt install -y stress-ng Generate CPU load for a short period:
stress-ng --cpu 2 --timeout 60s While the test is running:
Open the Grafana dashboard. Observe the CPU utilization graph. Check whether CPU usage increases during the test. Wait for the workload to finish. Verify that CPU usage returns toward its normal level. After the test, check that Prometheus continues to report both monitoring targets as UP.
Image 10: Generate CPU Load for Monitoring
Image 11: Monitor CPU Usage in Grafana
Conclusion In this section, we deployed a centralized monitoring solution using Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana on an AWS EC2 instance.
Node Exporter collects Linux server metrics, Prometheus stores and processes the metrics, and Grafana visualizes the monitoring data through dashboards.
The monitoring solution helps administrators observe server resource utilization, identify abnormal performance, and evaluate the operational status of the cloud infrastructure.
In the next section, we will test the Hybrid Cloud system and clean up AWS resources.

title: Hybrid Cloud System Testing and AWS Resource Cleanup
content:
Overview In this final section, we will verify the operation of the Hybrid Cloud system connecting the multi-branch enterprise network simulated in EVE-NG with the AWS cloud environment.
The testing process covers network connectivity, Site-to-Site VPN tunnels, routing and failover mechanisms, EC2 server availability, and the centralized monitoring solution using Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana.
After completing the tests, we will review the AWS resources and clean up resources that are no longer required to reduce unnecessary costs.
1. Review the Hybrid Cloud Architecture Before testing, review the overall system architecture and confirm that all required components have been deployed.
The system consists of:
On-premises infrastructure: Enterprise network simulated using EVE-NG, including headquarters and branch office networks. AWS VPC: Cloud network using CIDR 10.100.0.0/16. Virtual Private Gateway: Provides the AWS endpoint for Site-to-Site VPN connections. Customer Gateways: Represent the on-premises VPN devices. VPN connections: Provide encrypted connectivity between the enterprise network and AWS. EC2 instance: Hosts the web server and monitoring components. Monitoring system: Uses Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana to monitor server performance. Image 1: Overall Hybrid Cloud Architecture
2. Test Network Connectivity Verify communication between the on-premises enterprise network and the AWS VPC.
From an authorized on-premises host or router, test connectivity to the private IP address of the EC2 instance.
Example:
ping <EC2_PRIVATE_IP> Replace <EC2_PRIVATE_IP> with the actual private IP address of the EC2 instance.
Also verify that the routing table contains the expected routes to the AWS VPC:
show ip route 10.100.0.0 Check that the traffic is forwarded through the intended VPN path.
If connectivity fails, review the following:
AWS route table entries. On-premises routing configuration. VPN tunnel status. Security Group inbound rules. Network ACL rules, if customized. Host firewall configuration. Image 2: Test Connectivity from the Enterprise Network to AWS
3. Verify Site-to-Site VPN Connections Open the AWS VPC console and navigate to Site-to-Site VPN Connections.
Select each VPN connection and inspect the Tunnel details tab.
Verify that the expected VPN tunnels are operational and that the status is UP.
On the on-premises routers, use the following Cisco IOS commands:
show crypto isakmp sa show crypto ipsec sa show interface tunnel Check that the IPsec security associations are established and that traffic counters increase when communication occurs between the enterprise network and AWS.
Image 3: AWS Site-to-Site VPN Tunnel Status
4. Test Routing and VPN Failover Verify that the primary and backup VPN paths operate according to the routing design.
The expected behavior is:
Router15 provides the preferred primary VPN path. Router16 provides the backup path. The backup path is used when the primary path becomes unavailable. The primary path is preferred again after it recovers. Check the routing and tracking status:
show ip route 10.100.0.0 show track 100 show ip sla statistics Perform a controlled failover test:
Confirm that the primary VPN path is operational. Record the current routing table. Temporarily disable the primary path in the lab. Verify that the tracking mechanism detects the failure. Confirm that traffic uses the backup path. Restore the primary path. Verify that the original route preference is recovered. Do not perform this test during normal production operation without an approved maintenance window.
Image 4: Verify Primary and Backup VPN Routing
5. Test the EC2 Web Server Verify that the EC2 instance and its web server are operating correctly.
Check the Nginx service on Ubuntu:
sudo systemctl status nginx If Nginx is not running, start the service:
sudo systemctl start nginx Check that the web server is listening on port 80:
sudo ss -tulpn | grep :80 From an authorized browser, access:
http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP> Confirm that the web page is displayed successfully.
Also verify that the EC2 instance is in the Running state in the AWS EC2 console.
Image 5: Verify EC2 Instance Status
Image 6: Access the Nginx Web Server
6. Verify the Centralized Monitoring System Check the status of Node Exporter, Prometheus, and Grafana on the EC2 instance.
Run:
sudo systemctl status node_exporter sudo systemctl status prometheus sudo systemctl status grafana-server Open the Prometheus Targets page:
http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>:9090/targets Confirm that the prometheus and node_exporter targets are UP.
Then open Grafana:
http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>:3000 Verify that the monitoring dashboard displays server metrics such as:
CPU utilization. Memory utilization. Disk usage. Network traffic. Confirm that the graphs are receiving updated data from Prometheus.
Image 7: Prometheus Targets Verification
Image 8: Centralized Monitoring Dashboard
7. Review AWS Resource Usage and Costs Before cleaning up the environment, review the resources that may generate charges.
Open the AWS Management Console and check the following services:
EC2: Check running instances and attached storage volumes. Elastic IP addresses: Check allocated addresses that are not associated with running resources. EBS Volumes: Check volumes that are no longer required. Snapshots: Review snapshots that are no longer needed. VPN Connections: Review active Site-to-Site VPN connections. NAT Gateway: Check whether any NAT Gateway is deployed. CloudWatch: Review any monitoring resources that may incur additional charges. You can also review estimated spending through Billing and Cost Management.
Important: Stopping an EC2 instance does not stop all related charges. EBS volumes and other retained resources may continue to incur costs. Public IPv4 addresses and VPN connections may also have separate charges.
Image 9: Review AWS Resources
8. Clean Up Unnecessary AWS Resources Only delete resources that are no longer required for the workshop.
Before deleting anything, save the required configuration files, screenshots, and test results.
The cleanup process may include:
EC2 Instance
If the instance is no longer needed:
Open the EC2 console. Select Instances. Select the workshop EC2 instance. Choose Instance state. Select Terminate instance only if the instance is no longer required. EBS Volumes and Snapshots
Open Volumes in the EC2 console. Review unattached volumes. Delete only volumes that are no longer required and have been backed up if necessary. Review snapshots and delete only unnecessary snapshots. Site-to-Site VPN Resources
If the VPN environment is no longer needed:
Open Site-to-Site VPN Connections. Delete the VPN connections that are no longer required. Review and delete unused Customer Gateways. Review the Virtual Private Gateway before detaching or deleting it. Other Resources
Review unused Elastic IP addresses, NAT Gateways, and other resources before deleting them.
Important: Do not delete shared resources or resources still used by another part of the project. Terminating an EC2 instance is irreversible for its instance storage, and associated resources may require separate cleanup.
Image 10: AWS Resource Cleanup
9. Final System Evaluation After completing the tests, evaluate the overall operation of the Hybrid Cloud system.
The evaluation should cover:
Connectivity between the on-premises network and AWS. Establishment and operation of Site-to-Site VPN tunnels. Correct route selection between primary and backup paths. Successful failover and recovery. Availability of the EC2 web server. Successful collection of server metrics by Prometheus. Visualization of monitoring data in Grafana. Review and cleanup of unnecessary AWS resources. The results should be recorded with screenshots and test evidence for the project report.
Image 11: Final Hybrid Cloud System Verification
Conclusion In this final section, we verified the operation of the Hybrid Cloud system connecting the multi-branch enterprise network simulated in EVE-NG with the AWS cloud environment.
The tests covered network connectivity, Site-to-Site VPN operation, routing and failover, EC2 web server availability, and centralized monitoring using Prometheus, Node Exporter, and Grafana.
We also reviewed AWS resource usage and identified resources that could be cleaned up to reduce unnecessary costs.
Through this workshop, we completed the design, deployment, monitoring, and evaluation of a Hybrid Cloud solution for connecting multi-branch enterprise networks to AWS.
